# Preface {.unnumbered}

Somewhere on your hard drive there is a folder with a paper in it, and in that
folder there is a file called `figure1.pdf`.

Where did it come from? Which script made it? Was that script the current version
of the script, or the one from before you fixed the bug in the data-generating
function? If a reviewer asks you to change the sample sizes from 50, 100 and 400
to 50, 100, 400 and 1000, how many things do you have to remember to rerun, and in
what order, before the number in the abstract is right again?

Most of us answer these questions with memory and discipline. Both work fine until
the project gets big, or a coauthor touches it, or you come back to it after eight
months. This tutorial is about answering them with a file instead.

A *workflow manager* is a program that you tell, once, which files depend on which
other files and what command turns one into the other. After that it will build
anything you ask for, run only what is actually out of date, and refuse to let a
figure in your manuscript be older than the code that made it (unless you explicitly override it which isn't easy to do).
This tutorial focuses on one particular workflow manager: [Snakemake](https://snakemake.readthedocs.io/).

## Who this is for

Statisticians and biostatisticians who write R, run simulations, and produce
manuscripts or analysis reports. You should be comfortable in R. You do **not**
need to know Python (Snakemake is written in Python, and its files are Python, but
you will need about five minutes' worth of it, all of which is explained), and you
do not need to have used `make` or any other build tool.

Everything here runs on a laptop. However, one of Snakemake's (many) party tricks is that the same
workflow can be dispatched to a cluster by adding a configuration file and
changing nothing else, but that is out of scope; @sec-next points at where to read
about it when you need it.

## What we build

One example runs through most of the book. It is a small simulation study of a
problem every biostatistician has been asked about: what happens to confidence
intervals when the model was chosen using the same data.

In this example we will: generate data, select variables by forward selection, and compare the intervals
you get by naively refitting against the intervals you get by splitting the sample.
Then we compute this over a grid of sample sizes and correlation levels, turn the
results into a figure and a table, and compile the whole thing into a manuscript
--- so that changing one line of the simulation code and typing `snakemake`
rebuilds the PDF, correctly, every time.

By the end the pipeline looks like this:

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-align: center
flowchart LR
  C[code/sim.R] --> S1[18 simulation<br/>result files]
  S1 --> F[results/figure1.pdf]
  S1 --> T[results/table1.tex]
  F --> P[build/paper.pdf]
  T --> P
  M[main.tex] --> P
  M --> R[build/submission.pdf]
  F --> R
  T --> R
```

@sec-analysis then applies the same ideas to a piece of applied collaborative work --- raw
CSV, cleaning, models, Table 1, rendered report --- for readers whose focus is
analysis rather than methods research (most of us). I focus on the manuscript pipeline here because it parallels where I learned Snakemake, in my dissertation work.

## Installing Snakemake

Snakemake is a Python package. Once you have a Python setup you like, install
it there. E.g.:

```bash
python3 -m pip install snakemake
```

Check that it worked:

```bash
snakemake --version
```

This "book" was written against Snakemake 9.13. Version 8 introduced a number of
changes to how cluster execution is configured, and a few flags used here do not
exist in version 7 or earlier.

You will also want R with `optparse` and `ggplot2`; @sec-manuscript additionally
uses `tidyr`, `kableExtra` and a LaTeX installation, and @sec-analysis uses
`knitr` and Quarto. Each example's `README.md` lists what it needs.

## Getting the examples

Every code block in this book is printed from a file in the `examples/` directory
of [the tutorial repository](https://github.com/lharris421/snakemake-tutorial),
and every terminal transcript is pasted from a real run of that code. Nothing here
is pseudocode. Clone the repository and follow along:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/lharris421/snakemake-tutorial.git
cd snakemake-tutorial/examples/01-first-rules
snakemake --cores 2
```

The format and spirit of this tutorial are modeled on the [University of Iowa
